docs.text: ShapeTensor ¶ Fibre orientation fields of high-resolution white-matter volumes, from a pretrained shape-feature space, on the GPU. Tractography on microscopy-scale volumes (hierarchical phase-contrast X-ray tomography, HiP-CT, at 20 µm; serial histology; light-sheet) starts from a local orientation at every voxel. The standard estimate is the structure tensor : the direction of least gradient energy in a window. It is accurate and cheap, and it has two systematic failures that go straight into streamlines: at a tissue interface the gradients of the step overwhelm those of the fibre texture and the direction is dragged into the plane of the boundary; where bundles cross a single tensor can only report the bisector. ShapeTensor replaces the intensity with a pretrained 3-D network's shape features and runs one pipeline: Shape features — a contrast-agnostic 3-D UNet (anatomix), read at the encoder layer whose channels encode fibre orientation. Separating populations in the shape space — the orientation code is read without labels (the structure tensor at confident sites is the teacher), the populations present are the modes of the window's orientation distribution, and every voxel is unmixed onto their signatures: one activation layer per population , a full-volume image of that population's shape. One tensor per population — the image's structure tensor with the gradients weighted by the population's activation. Merging — one vector per voxel from the merged population tensors, or every population's vector with its activation as weight. No masks: the weights say where a population is present. import shapetensor as st vec = st.shapetensor(image, rho=10.0) # (3, Z, Y, X): one direction per voxel vecs = st.shapetensor(image, rho=10.0, multi=True) # (N, 3, Z, Y, X): every population, ordered by activation vec = st.structure_tensor(image, rho=10.0) # the excised structure tensor: the baseline The structure tensor it is compared with runs at the same σ and ρ as every tensor in the pipeline, and the boundary-robust ( excised ) structure tensor is the package's baseline and the pipeline's teacher. The idea, and the same stages on a 192³ block of HiP-CT: the image, its voxels in the shape space, the populations found there, their activation layers, each population's field, and the combined fields. Read the pipeline for each stage, parameters for what each setting does to the field, validation for what the phantoms show, and real data for HiP-CT and BigBrain. Status Version 0.2. The research notes behind every design decision, with all the numbers, are in the repository's notes/ directory; the documentation keeps to what the package does and what has been verified.

docs.text: Real data ¶ Two volumes are used throughout: a HiP-CT crop of human white matter at 20 µm, and a BigBrain volume of interest at 20 µm. On real data there is no truth; what is shown is the agreement between the fields, their behaviour at the structures the phantoms model (interfaces, crossings), and the streamlines they give. HiP-CT (S-21-46, 20 µm) ¶ A 768³ crop of a dehydrated human brain imaged by hierarchical phase-contrast tomography: white matter is bright, fibres darken it, the grey/white boundary and vessels are steps of 40–70 grey levels. The phantoms' texture (fibre density, widths, darkening, noise, dispersion) is matched to this crop ( shapetensor stats ). The same columns as every figure in the package: the image, the excised structure tensor, the shape space with the populations found in it, their activation layers, the single field and the first vector of the multi-vector field. The block's own structure tensor is the pipeline's teacher: calibrated on the 384³ around the block, the readout covers 18 of 24 orientation bins and two populations are found. The single field and the excised structure tensor agree to 7° where the tensor is confident (the top quarter by gap; 92% of those voxels within 15°) and to 13° over the whole block, which is low-coherence tissue (median gap 0.2) — the activation weights are what tells a consumer which voxels to trust. The population count on this block is sensitive to the detection settings ( parameters ): the two readings of the tissue differ by 8° at the median. BigBrain (20 µm) ¶ A 768³ volume of interest from the BigBrain histological reconstruction (a cell-body stain), resampled to 20 µm: white matter is dark and nearly featureless at this stain, so it is the harder case for any gradient-based estimate and a test of the engine on a different contrast; the pipeline reads three populations in it, which with no truth is a statement about the shape space of this stain, not about fibres. scripts/bigbrain_fetch.py downloads it. Other scales, other regions, a whole brain ¶ Scales and regions : the same pipeline on HiP-CT from 2.2 µm to 200 µm voxels, on four regions of S-21-46 at 20 µm, and over a whole brain at 100 µm. Anisotropic voxels ¶ Both the structure tensor and the pipeline take spacing=(dz, dy, dx) ; the shape engine resamples the block to isotropic voxels internally. On 20 × 20 × 50 µm data, fibres that run perpendicular to the coarse axis lose their across-fibre contrast in the sampling itself, and no filtering recovers it; sample isotropically at the texture scale where you can.

docs.text: Installation ¶ ShapeTensor is a Python package (3.11+) on PyTorch with CUDA. Everything computes on the GPU. git clone https://github.com/Andrew-Keenlyside/ShapeTensor.git cd ShapeTensor pip install -e . # numpy, scipy, torch, zarr >= 3, matplotlib pip install -e ".[anatomix]" # the shape-feature network (anatomix, monai); weights come from the HF hub on first use pip install -e ".[dev]" # pytest Install a CUDA build of torch matching your driver first if pip would not pick one (for example pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124 ). anatomix's package metadata pins a newer torch than it needs; if the resolver complains, pip install --no-deps git+https://github.com/neel-dey/anatomix.git huggingface_hub . The weights ( neeldey/anatomix ) are cached under HF_HOME . Memory ¶ The feature engine runs the network on tiles of 256³ with 64 voxels of context; a pass needs about 10 GB at the encoder layer the pipeline reads. The pipeline on a 192³ block peaks at about 10 GB, on 256³ at about 22 GB. On a 24 GB card use --chunk 128 128 128 --calibration-size 192 ; shapetensor bench reports the times and the peak memory on your GPU. There is no CPU fallback. Container ¶ envs/shapetensor-gpu.def builds an Apptainer image (PyTorch 2.5.1 / CUDA 12.4, the weights baked in): apptainer build --fakeroot shapetensor-gpu.sif envs/shapetensor-gpu.def apptainer exec --nv shapetensor-gpu.sif shapetensor run in.ome.zarr out.zarr --level 0 --rho 10 Data root ¶ Phantoms and results of the validation go under SHAPETENSOR_DATA (default ~/shapetensor_data ). Tests ¶ pytest tests # the structure tensor against scipy; the pipeline's pieces; the whole pipeline on a phantom (GPU) shapetensor demo # the install check: a crossing phantom through the whole pipeline Seeds are fixed, but the readout's training steps on the GPU are not bit-reproducible, so a borderline population decision can differ between two runs on the same block.

docs.text: Parameters ¶ What each parameter does to the field, one at a time, on the HiP-CT block of real data (S-21-46, 20 µm, a 192³ block calibrated on the 384³ around it), the rest at their defaults. Every strip shows the shape tensor's single field as DEC colour (R = |x|, G = |y|, B = |z|) at every voxel. The titles give the populations found and the median angle of the field from the default run's over the tissue. python scripts/parameters.py # docs/img/params_<name>.png, results/parameters.json Two things are not parameters: the feature layer (encoder block 2 of anatomix, the layer where orientation is a linear code) and the teacher (the excised structure tensor at the output rho ). Changing the scale at which the shape is read means resampling the image; see the pipeline . What the strips show overall: the field's direction is set by the scales and by which populations are found, and by nothing else. The weight floor and the sub-window size leave it unchanged; a different population count or a different pair of populations moves it by 9–16° at the median on this low-coherence block, where several readings of the tissue are plausible. The readout's fit is not bit-reproducible on the GPU, so the exact populations a run finds, and these numbers, vary a little between runs. The scales: rho and sigma ¶ rho is the integration window of every tensor: the teacher, each population's tensor and the baseline structure tensor. It is the one scale a user should normally touch. Smaller windows follow the fibres more closely and carry more noise (the structure tensor's swirl defects at ρ 5, three populations found); larger ones smooth the field and blur crossings and bends further. The bottom row is the excised structure tensor at the same rho : the two fields move together, which is what makes the comparison like for like. At ρ 20 the teacher is smoother than the fascicles of this block and one population is found. sigma is the derivative scale. At half a voxel the gradients see the noise and the teacher, and so the field, change character (24° from the default); at two voxels the fibre texture (period about 5 voxels at 20 µm) is blurred before it is differentiated, every tensor loses contrast and one population is found. The feature average: smooth ¶ The features are box-averaged over smooth ³ voxels before the readers are fitted and before the activations are thresholded for the tissue mask. The activation of a rectified filter oscillates with the phase of the fibre texture; a 3³ average (the default) integrates it. Without it the activations spike voxel by voxel, the null is lower and the second population is not confirmed; a 5³ box blurs the layers at the scale of the box and leaves the field within 3° of the default. Finding the populations: nmax , min_sep_deg , window , iterations ¶ These decide how many populations the block is unmixed onto, not how any tensor integrates. The top row is the single field; the bottom row is the second vector of the multi-vector field with its activation as brightness, black where only one population was found. nmax caps the number of populations. With one population the single field is the excised structure tensor weighted by that population's activation (15° from the default here). With two the block has two readings that differ by 9°: the default (candidates from the 64³ sub-windows, up to three confirmed) and the pair found with nmax 2 or window 0, which is the same pair. min_sep_deg is the angle below which two candidate populations are the same one. Smaller values let the shoulders of one dispersed population count as two (at 15° a different pair is found, 16° from the default); at 40° the two populations of this block are merged into one. window is the size of the sub-windows in which candidate populations are looked for, 0 for the block only. A population confined to one region of the block is found through its sub-window; 64 and 96 give the same result here. iterations is the number of joint refinements of the populations from their own layers after the candidates are confirmed one by one. One pass or four leave the field within 4–5° of the default on this block. Little or no effect on the field: tensor_floor , tissue ¶ tensor_floor is the weight floor of every population tensor, as a fraction of the null. It keeps a population's tensor defined where its activation is zero and is not a lever on the field (0.3° between 0 and 0.1; also notes/results_log.md §27). tissue is the optional mask of the voxels to read (here the grey level above the air/tissue threshold). It chooses where the teacher is sampled and where the excision looks for steps; it is never applied to the vectors, and on a block that is all tissue it changes the field by 4°.

docs.text: These decide how many populations the block is unmixed onto, not how any tensor integrates. The top row is the single field; the bottom row is the second vector of the multi-vector field with its activation as brightness, black where only one population was found. nmax caps the number of populations. With one population the single field is the excised structure tensor weighted by that population's activation (15° from the default here). With two the block has two readings that differ by 9°: the default (candidates from the 64³ sub-windows, up to three confirmed) and the pair found with nmax 2 or window 0, which is the same pair. min_sep_deg is the angle below which two candidate populations are the same one. Smaller values let the shoulders of one dispersed population count as two (at 15° a different pair is found, 16° from the default); at 40° the two populations of this block are merged into one. window is the size of the sub-windows in which candidate populations are looked for, 0 for the block only. A population confined to one region of the block is found through its sub-window; 64 and 96 give the same result here. iterations is the number of joint refinements of the populations from their own layers after the candidates are confirmed one by one. One pass or four leave the field within 4–5° of the default on this block.

docs.text: tensor_floor is the weight floor of every population tensor, as a fraction of the null. docs.text: Scales, regions, a whole brain ¶ The same pipeline, at the same settings (σ 1, ρ 10 voxels, calibration on the 384³ around a 192³ block, tissue = grey level above zero), on HiP-CT at six voxel sizes, on four regions of one brain at 20 µm, and over a whole brain at 100 µm. There is no truth on real data; what is reported is what the pipeline finds, and how far its single field is from the excised structure tensor at the same scales, over the tissue and where the tensor is confident (its top quarter by orientation gap). Every direction field is drawn as plain DEC at every voxel, the shape tensor's exactly as the structure tensor's. python scripts/scales.py # docs/img/scales.png, docs/img/regions_20um.png, results/scales.json python scripts/wholebrain.py run # the 100 µm brain: shape.zarr and st.zarr under /hdd/andrew/shapetensor_runs python scripts/wholebrain.py figure # docs/img/wholebrain_100um.png, results/wholebrain_100um.json Six voxel sizes ¶ The two finest blocks are from I74 (a 2.2 µm volume of interest and a 10 µm chunk); the four coarser ones are the deep brain of S-21-46, at 20 µm from its 20 µm scan and at 50, 100 and 200 µm from the levels of its 50 µm scan, centred on the same thalamic site. The parameters are in voxels, so the integration window runs from 22 µm to 2 mm down the figure and the network's 16-voxel receptive field from 35 µm to 3.2 mm. From 20 µm to 100 µm the pipeline reads the deep brain as two populations and its single field is within 5° of the excised tensor where the tensor is confident (6° to 12° over the block). At 50 µm the activation layers follow the fascicles that are visible in the image, one layer per direction of fibre bundle. At 200 µm the receptive field is 3 mm and the three "populations" are tissue classes: a band of white matter, the oriented edge of the ventricle, the rest. The field still agrees with the tensor (14°, 7° where confident), because both are now reading anatomy, not fibres. At 2.2 µm and 10 µm the voxels resolve cells, vessels and single axons. The features are read at a receptive field of 35 µm and 160 µm, the readers calibrate on whatever is oriented at that scale (a vessel is one of the three populations at 2.2 µm), and the single field departs from the structure tensor by 20° to 25°. The pipeline reads shape at the scale of its receptive field; the voxel size decides what a "fibre" is. For sub-cellular voxel sizes, downsample to the fascicle scale first. Four regions at 20 µm ¶ Deep brain, a gyral white-matter site, the brainstem and the cerebellar white matter of S-21-46, each a 192³ block. Two things the figure settles about calibration. Self-calibration needs orientation diversity. The brainstem block's fibres run in one direction, its teacher occupies 7 of 24 orientation bins, the readers cannot learn an orientation code from one orientation, and the null rises until a third of the tissue is above it. The field is then the excised tensor weighted by a degenerate activation (2.5° from the tensor, weights that mean little). A calibration does not travel. The third row applies the deep-brain block's calibration to the other three regions: the cortex block goes from 13° to 32° from the tensor with 45% of its tissue above the null, the brainstem from 2.5° to 18° with 9% above, the cerebellum stays at 19° to 25°. The readers are specific to the local texture (its feature statistics, its signatures); a calibration from elsewhere in the same brain reads a region's populations poorly. So the rule for a volume is calibrate every chunk on itself , and fall back to a volume calibration only where a chunk's teacher covers too few orientations. That is what run_volume now does ( calibrate_chunks , min_bins ); one calibration for the whole volume remains an option. A whole brain at 100 µm ¶ S-21-46 at 100 µm (1475 × 1493 × 1493 voxels, level 1 of its 50 µm scan), in 256³ chunks each calibrated on itself (the central 256³'s calibration as fallback), the chunks' merged tensors ramp-blended over a 32-voxel overlap at every face, chunks without tissue skipped, and the excised structure tensor over the same volume at the same σ and ρ (1 mm integration). The weights are zero where the masked volume has no data; the vectors are never masked. Every field is drawn as plain DEC. 121 chunks of 256³ held tissue, 95 were air and skipped; 114 chunks used their own calibration and 7 the volume's (a teacher with too few orientations, or too little oriented tissue to fit on). No chunk failed, and the field has no seams. On the three mid planes the single field is 8° from the excised tensor over the tissue and 4° where the tensor is confident. The shape pass took 2 hours at a median of 62 s per chunk (the per-chunk calibration, the overlap and the accumulators on top of the 26 s of stages 2–4), the blended write 6 minutes and the structure tensor 5 minutes. The two fields agree on the large structure, the corpus callosum, the internal capsule, the cerebellar peduncles; the shape tensor is the finer-grained of the two, following the gyral white matter and the cortex at the scale of its receptive field (1.6 mm here) where the structure tensor's 1 mm window has already averaged it.

docs.text: The structure tensor, the baseline ¶ The structure tensor of a volume is the window average of the outer product of its gradient: \[S = G_\rho * \left(\nabla I_\sigma\, \nabla I_\sigma^{\mathsf T}\right)\] with the gradient at scale σ and the average over a window ρ. The fibre direction is the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue — the direction along which the intensity changes least — and the orientation gap (λ₂ − λ₃) / λ₂ is how unique that direction is. shapetensor.st computes it on the GPU in the layout of the structure-tensor package, so its outputs substitute wherever that package's are consumed. from shapetensor import st S = st.structure_tensor_3d(image, 1.0, 10.0) # (6, Z, Y, X) = [Sxx, Syy, Szz, Sxy, Sxz, Syz] val, vec = st.eig_special_3d(S) # eigenvalues (descending); the smallest's eigenvector, (x, y, z) vec = st.structure_tensor(image, rho=10.0) # the same in one call, excised (below) Where it fails ¶ At a tissue interface — the grey/white boundary, the edge of a tract, a vessel wall — the gradients of the step overwhelm those of the fibre texture inside the window, and the direction is dragged into the plane of the boundary: streamlines wrap along it. The size of the effect is the ratio of the step to the texture; at the real tissue's texture level, next to a step of 40 grey levels, it is tens of degrees within 0.1 mm of the boundary. Where bundles cross , a single tensor reports the bisector, whatever the window. The excised structure tensor ¶ The interface failure has a direct remedy inside the tensor: leave the boundary's gradients out. Gradients whose coarse magnitude (σ = 3 voxels) exceeds three times the median are given zero weight and the window average is renormalised by the surviving weight. Nothing changes in clear tissue (the test suite checks that a block with no step is untouched), and at a step the error drops to the clear-tissue level. The excised structure tensor is the package's baseline, its default structure_tensor , the teacher of the pipeline's stage 2, and the excision is built into every population tensor of stage 3. Sx = st.excised_structure_tensor_3d(image, 1.0, 10.0, factor=3.0, mask=tissue) mask is the tissue over which the reference median is taken (without it, the whole block; too low a reference where much of the block is smooth grey matter or background). A whole volume ¶ shapetensor structure-tensor brain.ome.zarr st.zarr --level 0 --rho 10 --chunk 256 256 256 writes S , val and vec chunk by chunk with halos; every chunk equals a one-pass computation (for the excised tensor the reference median is per chunk). Anisotropic voxels ¶ spacing=(dz, dy, dx) declares the voxel size per axis (for example (2.5, 1, 1) for 50 × 20 × 20 µm). The filters are scaled per axis and the gradients divided by the spacing, so the tensor and its directions are in physical coordinates. This is correct only while the coarse axis still resolves the fibre texture; where it does not (fibres running perpendicular to a 50 µm axis at 20 µm fibre spacing), no filtering recovers what the sampling destroyed, and isotropic sampling at the texture scale is the remedy.

docs.text: Validation on phantoms ¶ Three phantoms with truth, at 20 µm voxels, 192³ blocks with 32 voxels of context, three seeds each; every field at σ 1, ρ 10 voxels. The texture is the one matched to the real HiP-CT crop: 20° of fibre dispersion within a population and half the fibre darkening ( shapetensor stats ). The structure tensor (plain and excised) is scored against the shape tensor's single field and the first vector of its multi-vector field. shapetensor validate --out validation # validation.json, validation_calibrated.png The shape pipeline is calibrated once on twelve single bundles at 15° steps of orientation (a phantom block has one or two orientations, too few to calibrate on itself; a real block has them all). bundle — one population at 60°: the clear-tissue floor. crossing — two populations at 60°, equal density, interdigitated at the fascicle scale. interface — one population crossing a tissue step of 40 grey levels, at 90°, 60° and 30° to it in three bands. Each row is one phantom in the package's standard layout: the image, the excised structure tensor, the shape space with the populations found in it, one activation layer per population, the shape tensor's single field and the first vector of its multi-vector field, every field as plain DEC at every voxel, with each field's median error against the truth in its title. results/validation.json has every seed and every band. What it shows ¶ On the bundle both fields are within 4° of the truth; the shape tensor is the closer (2.4° against 3.9°), because the activation weighting discounts the voxels between fibres. At the crossing the structure tensor reports the bisector (24° from either population, 10% of voxels within 15°). The pipeline finds two populations on every seed. Its single field is also near the bisector (23°), as a merged tensor must be, but the first vector of the multi-vector field is 11.6° from the nearest population with 55% of voxels within 15°: at each voxel the stronger population's own tensor. The pair is not resolved per voxel (both vectors within 15° at 1% of voxels): with 20° of dispersion within each population the two activation layers overlap, and the second vector is indicative only. At the interface the plain structure tensor is dragged 35° into the step within 0.1 mm of it; the excision removes this (6°), and the pipeline inherits the excision. The shape tensor is nonetheless the noisier field here (17° against 6°, in every band): three bands at different angles to the step are read as one or two populations, and their activation weighting cannot sharpen three directions. Where a block holds one coherent direction the pipeline matches the excised tensor; where it holds several, the population count per region is the lever, not the weights ( notes/results_log.md §27). What to take from it ¶ The excision is the remedy for interfaces; it is in the baseline and inside every population tensor. At a crossing, use the multi-vector field's first vector where the two populations are of different strength, and treat the second as indicative. The single field is a merged tensor and reports the bisector like the structure tensor. Tight, coherent bundles (8° dispersion, the coherent setting of shapetensor validate --settings coherent ) are separated per voxel and were the earlier validation's headline; they are not the regime of the HiP-CT crop, so they are no longer the default and are not shown here. On the real block, where orientations vary smoothly, the single field agrees with the excised tensor to 7° where the tensor is confident ( real data ).

docs.text: 4. Merging the population fields ¶ Two outputs, both covering the whole volume, both carrying the activation as weight. No masks are applied : a mask would cut the field where a population fades, and a downstream consumer can weight or threshold as it needs. Where a population is absent its weight is at the noise level, and the null tau exported with every field says what that level is. One vector per voxel ¶ The merged population tensor, each population's tensor weighted by its activation: \[T = \sum_r a_r\, \frac{S_r}{\operatorname{tr} S_r}\] Its smallest eigenvector is the field's direction, its gap the uniqueness, the total activation its weight. A layer without a coherent direction has a near-isotropic tensor and adds none, so it is discounted by itself. This is the shape tensor's single field — the like-for-like alternative to the structure tensor's eigenvector. Several vectors per voxel ¶ Every population's direction at every voxel, ordered by activation, with the activation as weight ( vecs (N, 3, Z, Y, X) , weights (N, Z, Y, X) ). A streamline builder that follows the vector most aligned with its heading can use the weight as its confidence; where one population is present the others' weights sit at the noise level. out = st.population_field(image, rho=10.0) out["vec"], out["vec_gap"], out["weight"] # the single field out["vecs"], out["weights"], out["tau"] # the multi-vector field and the activation null Tissue and population masks, for those who want them ¶ For node sampling or display, tissue_mask is where the smoothed total activation exceeds the null, masks where each population's does, and strongest the index of the most active population inside the tissue mask. They are outputs, not steps: nothing in the vectors depends on them. At a chunk seam, and what the weights mean ¶ The chunked driver finds the populations of every chunk, and calibrates every chunk on itself, so the merged tensor differs from its neighbour's near their common face even though every voxel's tensors are exact; written side by side, the two readings meet in a visible seam. run_volume therefore overlaps neighbouring chunks by blend voxels (32) on each side of every face, accumulates each chunk's merged tensor — it is linear in the activations — with linear ramps that sum to 1 across the seam, and takes the field from the blended tensor, so one reading turns into the next over 64 voxels. The network and the filters see enough beyond the overlap for every blended tensor to be exact. The multi-vector field is written per chunk without blending: it is ordered by activation at every voxel, so its first vector means the same on both sides of a seam, but the set of populations may not. The activation weights of apply are in the standardised feature's units, normalised per direction; weight / tau is the dimensionless presence (above 1: present). run_volume writes the weight already divided by the chunk's null, so that chunks calibrated on themselves are comparable, and zero where the volume has no data. Displaying the field ¶ The field is a direction and a weight at every voxel, and how it is drawn is a choice made at display time, not in the pipeline. The figures in this documentation draw every direction field as plain DEC colour (R = |x|, G = |y|, B = |z|) at every voxel, the shape tensor's exactly as the structure tensor's, and show the activation as its own layers; the same field can also be drawn with the activation as brightness (linear or compressed), cut at the null, or over the grey image with the activation as opacity or as saturation ( shapetensor.viz.dec_rgb , dec_activation_overlay ; scripts/renderings.py , which redraws from a cached slice without the GPU): Orientation alone shows what the vectors say everywhere, including where nothing oriented is present; it is the honest comparison with the structure tensor's DEC, which also has a direction at every voxel. Brightness = activation is the field as a downstream consumer should weight it; the square root keeps the faint tissue readable when the scale is set by the strongest fascicles. Cut at the null is the tissue mask as a display; it is the one rendering that hides information. Over the image , opacity shows where the orientation is supported and what it is supported by; saturation keeps the image's anatomy legible and greys out the unsupported voxels. Following the field ¶ shapetensor.tracking.track is a deterministic streamline tracker over a multi-vector grid (nearest-vector, curvature-limited), the same code for every field, so that fields can be compared by their streamlines rather than by their vectors. Given the no-mask field's weights and a min_weight (the null tau ), it follows a vector only where its population is present. Real data shows the structure tensor's and the shape tensor's streamlines on the same HiP-CT block.

docs.text: 2. Separating populations in the shape space ¶ Stage 2 answers two questions without labels: which fibre populations are present in a window, and where each of them is, voxel by voxel. Its readers are fitted on the block itself. The teacher ¶ The excised structure tensor at the output ρ is the teacher: at its confident sites (the top 30% by orientation gap in the tissue, drawn evenly over orientation bins so that no direction dominates) its direction is taken as that voxel's orientation. No labels, no annotation. The least oriented 30% of the tissue give a background pattern. Two readers of the shape space ¶ The signature dictionary is the mean standardised feature pattern of every orientation (160 directions on a hemisphere, kernel-smoothed), plus the background pattern. The signature of any direction is interpolated from it. The orientation readout is a small network from a voxel's features to a distribution over the same 160 directions, trained with the teacher's direction as a soft target. Summed over a window, the voxels' distributions are the window's orientation density , whose peaks are the candidate populations. Both are fitted by shapetensor.pipeline.calibrate on one block (real data) or on a set of single-population blocks (phantoms at several orientations), and both are applied unchanged to any block of the same data. Which populations: candidates confirmed by their layers ¶ The readers do not respond equally to every direction (the network's filters are not isotropic), so both are gain-normalised per direction against the teacher on the calibration block: the density by the ratio of what the readout reports to the teacher's own orientation histogram, the activations by what a sample reaches on its own direction's signature. Every direction then counts alike. The density's peaks still over-count: a single population with dispersed fibres has shoulders that a peak finder reads as further populations. The pipeline therefore gathers up to six candidates — the peaks of the block's density and of its 64³ sub-windows' (a block may hold regions of different orientation) — and lets stage 3 judge them. Each candidate is first unmixed alone into its activation layer (below), and the layer's own population tensor — the image's gradients weighted by that activation — gives the direction its fibres actually have; the shoulders of one population all point at that population, a real second population points elsewhere, and the distinct axes (25° apart) are kept. The kept axes are then unmixed together , twice, and the distinct axes kept again: under a joint unmixing the shoulders lose their shared voxels to the population they belong to. A joint unmixing never has more than four signatures (the rank of the orientation code is five), and a population must own at least 5% of the tissue above the activation null. Where each population is: the activation layers ¶ Every voxel's feature vector is decomposed non-negatively onto the signatures of the populations found plus the background: \[x(v) \approx \sum_r a_r(v)\, D(\theta_r) + b(v)\, D_\text{bg}, \qquad a_r \ge 0\] The coefficients \(a_r(v)\) are the activation layers : one full-volume image per population of where that population's shape is, not a mask of the image. They are what stage 3 weights the image gradients with and what stage 4 uses as weights. The null \(\tau\) — the activation a wrong population's signature reaches on single-population voxels, calibrated on the block — is exported with every field; it is never applied to the vectors. The crossing row of the validation figure shows the layers on a phantom; the real data figures show them on HiP-CT and BigBrain. What this stage cannot do ¶ With the second-order orientation code of the features (stage 1), a voxel whose receptive field holds two populations looks like a weaker single population at their bisector, and three populations are linearly dependent. Separation therefore works where the populations interdigitate at the fascicle scale, and it degrades as the crossing angle closes and as the fibres within a population disperse: see validation .

docs.text: 1. Shape features ¶ The block goes through anatomix , a contrast-agnostic 3-D UNet pretrained for registration across modalities, and the pipeline reads its encoder block 2 : 32 channels at half resolution (upsampled to the grid), a receptive field of 16 voxels (0.32 mm at 20 µm). This is the layer where orientation is encoded as a linear code: the mean feature pattern of an oriented voxel is a linear image of its orientation dyad d dᵀ to 98% on phantoms and 79% on a real block ( notes/results_log.md §26). Deeper layers (the decoder's layer 58, the output) lose the per-fascicle division: their receptive fields average crossing populations into the bisector before anything can be read. from shapetensor.features import make_engine F = make_engine("anatomix_enc2")(block) # (32, Z, Y, X) The engine runs the network on tiles of 256³ with 64 voxels of real context on every face and keeps only each tile's core, with reflect padding of the block (the network's own zero padding would put a step at the faces). Its output is unreliable within 24 voxels of a block face; the pipeline's calibration never samples there. Two other engines exist for comparison: jet , a multiscale Gaussian derivative jet without any network (the control arm), and the deeper anatomix layers anatomix48 and anatomix16 . What the features are, and what they are not ¶ A channel of encoder block 2 is a rectified (ReLU) filter response. It is zero over much of the texture and responds where its filter lands on a fibre edge in phase , so a per-voxel read of these features oscillates with the fibre texture (on a fibre / between fibres) the way the raw gradient energy does; the structure tensor is smooth because it squares the gradient and integrates over ρ. The pipeline therefore averages the features over 3³ before any read-out ( smooth ), and every tensor it builds integrates over ρ as the baseline does. No root or log of the features or of the activations can replace that integration: a pointwise transform moves no power between spatial frequencies ( notes/results_log.md §25). The orientation content of a voxel's features is of second order in the direction — the same content as a structure tensor at the receptive-field scale, with a learned amplitude. That sets what stage 2 can and cannot separate: two populations, yes; a 50/50 mixture at Δθ looks like a weaker single population at the bisector; a third population is linearly dependent on two.

Its tensor is the image's structure tensor with every gradient weighted by the activation and by the boundary excision, integrated over the same window ρ as the baseline and normalised by the integrated weight: \[S_r = \frac{G_\rho * \left(a_r\, w\, \nabla I\, \nabla I^{\mathsf T}\right)}{G_\rho * (a_r\, w)}\] Where the population is present its own fibres' gradients make the tensor, and only those; elsewhere the weight is at the noise level.
